events.x: When soldiers came to enforce the exile of Grenoble’s parlement, townspeople climbed onto the roofs and pelted them with tiles. The riot led to the Assembly of Vizille, where the province’s three estates met without the king’s leave.
pic: Journée des Tuiles (Alexandre Debelle), Musée de la Révolution française - Vizille.jpg
m: jhZjzA1w5dk
On 7 June 1788 Grenoble rises against troops sent to remove its judges; tiles rain from rooftops, soldiers fire, and rioters take over the town.
jhZjzA1w5dk
Ambitious young judge Jean-Joseph Mounier calls the Vizille assembly, which demands provincial estates, a doubled Third Estate and voting together in a single chamber.

events.x: A rumor that the wallpaper maker Jean-Baptiste Réveillon wanted wages cut set off a riot in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine. Crowds sacked his house and works; troops fired on them, and dozens or more were killed.
m: gxrk1Tlbgd4
A false rumor about wages targets Réveillon, a self-made wallpaper manufacturer in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine who backed the first balloon flights and paid workers well.
gxrk1Tlbgd4
A crowd of thousands wrecks and burns Réveillon's house and workshop; troops fire, killing perhaps 300, the bloodiest day until 1792.

events.x: About 1,200 deputies of the clergy, the nobility and the commoners met at Versailles, the first Estates General since 1614. The Third Estate wanted all three orders to sit and vote together.
pic: Opening of the Estates General at Versailles on 5th May 1789.jpg
m: gxrk1Tlbgd4
The royal procession through Versailles to the church of Saint-Louis displays the social hierarchy, with the Third Estate trailing behind in plain black.
gxrk1Tlbgd4
At the opening session the Third Estate sits at the back, a hat-doffing muddle follows the king's speech, and Necker's long finance address bores everyone.

events.x: Locked out of their hall, the deputies of the new National Assembly met in a nearby indoor tennis court and swore not to part until France had a constitution.
ppl: Honoré Gabriel Riqueti, comte de Mirabeau
pic: Serment du Jeu de Paume - Jacques-Louis David.jpg
m: gxrk1Tlbgd4
Necker urges concessions, the queen and royal brothers want a crackdown; Louis plans a royal session, and on 20 June deputies find their hall shut.
gxrk1Tlbgd4
Guillotin finds a nearby real-tennis court where, at Mounier's urging and echoing David's Horatii, deputies swear not to part until France has a constitution.

events.x: Louis XVI sacked his popular finance minister and ordered him to leave France at once. With some 20,000 troops gathering around Paris, many Parisians took it as the start of a crackdown.
pic: Necker, Jacques, par Boillet, BNF Gallica.jpg
m: gxrk1Tlbgd4
Late on 11 July Louis dismisses Necker and orders him out of France; a noble deputy warns his wife in Paris to stay in.
70hIVrErUJg
Louis XVI abruptly dismisses the popular finance minister Necker, who heads to Brussels yet still pledges his own fortune to guarantee food shipments.

events.t: Call to arms at the Palais-Royal
events.x: As news of Necker’s fall reached the crowds in the Palais-Royal gardens, the young journalist Camille Desmoulins jumped onto a café table and called Parisians to arms. Marchers then paraded wax busts of Necker and the Duke of Orléans.
ppl: Louis Philippe II, Duke of Orléans
m: 70hIVrErUJg
Desmoulins urges the crowd to arm and wear green leaves; marchers in mourning shut theatres and parade wax busts of Necker and Orléans.

events.at: Place Louis XV and the Tuileries Garden
events.x: German-speaking cavalry tried to clear the crowd from Place Louis XV and rode into the Tuileries Garden. French Guards took the crowd’s side, and the royal commander, Besenval, pulled his troops out of Paris.
ppl: Pierre Victor, baron de Besenval de Brünstatt
m: 70hIVrErUJg
German cavalry clash with protesters at Place Vendôme and the Tuileries; French Guards join the crowd and Besenval withdraws royal troops from Paris.

events.x: On the morning of the 14th, a huge crowd broke into the Invalides and carried off muskets and cannon. They had no gunpowder, and the nearest store of it was in the Bastille.
m: 70hIVrErUJg
Flesselles sends arms-seekers on fruitless errands, fuelling suspicion; on 14 July a vast crowd storms the Invalides for muskets and cannon but finds no powder.

events.x: After hours of fighting, the fortress’s small garrison gave up to the crowd and to French Guards who had brought cannon. Only seven prisoners were inside. The governor, de Launay, was killed on the way to the Hôtel de Ville.
m: 70hIVrErUJg
Impatient besiegers storm the outer courtyard, cut down a drawbridge that crushes one man, then come under fire and suspect a deliberate trap.
70hIVrErUJg
Hulin brings French Guards with cannon; de Launay threatens to blow the magazine, but his garrison objects and he surrenders by late afternoon.
70hIVrErUJg
Instead of martyrs the victors find just seven inmates, forgers, a libertine count and two madmen, and parade a bewildered bearded lunatic through Paris.
70hIVrErUJg
Captured, de Launay is dragged to City Hall, killed by the mob and beheaded by the cook Desnot; suspected traitor Flesselles meets the same fate.

events.x: Three days after the Bastille fell, Louis XVI rode into Paris. At the Hôtel de Ville the new mayor, Bailly, gave him the new cockade, and he put it in his hat.
m: 70hIVrErUJg
Louis travels plainly to Paris, receives the city's keys from Bailly with a pointed Henry IV comparison, and accepts the tricolour cockade at City Hall.
Ey4xBrSKMAw
Louis's tricolour cockade joins royal white to Paris's blue and red, the colours of Saints Martin and Denis, tying the new order to ancient legend.

events.x: A crowd seized Joseph Foullon, a royal official said to have told the hungry to eat hay, and his son-in-law Bertier de Sauvigny, the intendant of Paris. Both were killed outside the Hôtel de Ville.
ppl: Louis Bénigne François Bertier de Sauvigny
m: 70hIVrErUJg
A week later crowds lynch Foullon and his son-in-law Bertier de Sauvigny, killings Loustalot's paper defends, signalling that revolutionary violence has only begun.

events.x: Alarmed by peasant risings across the countryside, the National Assembly voted away feudal dues, the nobles’ privileges and the tithe in a single night.
m: Ey4xBrSKMAw
On the evening of 4 August 1789 the Vicomte de Noailles, Lafayette's brother-in-law and Yorktown veteran, proposes ending feudal obligations and making everyone pay taxes.
Ey4xBrSKMAw
Swept up in enthusiasm, clergy and nobles trade sacrifices, a bishop targeting hunting rights and a duke tithes, until privilege itself falls overnight.

events.at: From the Hôtel de Ville to Versailles
events.x: Thousands of Paris market women, angry at the price of bread, walked twelve miles in the rain to Versailles, with Lafayette and the National Guard behind them. Before dawn the next day, part of the crowd broke into the palace.
m: xDbI4Pi6dXs
Summoned by drum and bells, thousands of market women seize arms and cannon at the Hôtel de Ville and march on Versailles in the rain.
xDbI4Pi6dXs
Some 15,000 National Guards insist on following the women, and a reluctant Lafayette rides at their head, carried along by his own men.
xDbI4Pi6dXs
Repulsed at the palace, the soaked women invade the Assembly; their delegate Louison Chabry faints before Louis, who promises grain and accepts the decrees outright.
xDbI4Pi6dXs
At dawn the crowd breaks in and kills guards at the queen's door; Marie Antoinette escapes barefoot through a hidden passage to the king's rooms.

events.t: The royal family taken to Paris
events.x: The crowd made the king, the queen and their children leave Versailles for Paris, escorted by National Guards and marchers. They moved into the Tuileries Palace, and the Assembly soon followed them to Paris.
m: xDbI4Pi6dXs
Lafayette wakes, calms the crowd, and brings Louis onto the balcony to agree to go to Paris, pinning a tricolour cockade on a royal bodyguard.
xDbI4Pi6dXs
Led by the guards' heads on pikes, a seven-hour procession takes the silent royals to the Hôtel de Ville and the Tuileries, where Fersen waits.
xDbI4Pi6dXs
After the October Days the Assembly strips the king of key powers, then itself moves to Paris, exposed to factions and pressure from the crowds.

events.x: On the first anniversary of the Bastille, delegates from all over France met on the Champ de Mars, which Parisians had dug into a vast arena by hand. Lafayette led an oath to the nation, the law and the king.
pic: Fête de la Fédération 1790, Musée de la Révolution française - Vizille.jpg
m: Dbvk5N9Pe84
Barnave's moderates want a settlement with Louis, who looks cooperative after his plain-coated oath at the July 1790 Fête de la Fédération.

events.x: The royal family slipped out of the Tuileries at night in disguise, heading for loyal troops at Montmédy. The postmaster Drouet recognized the king at Sainte-Menehould, and the family was stopped at Varennes and taken back to Paris.
pic: Le roi reconnu à chalons par Dumont.jpg
m: Dbvk5N9Pe84
Louis walks calmly out past the guards, Marie Antoinette narrowly avoids Lafayette, and Fersen drives the reunited family to the Saint-Martin barrier.
Dbvk5N9Pe84
The bodyguards' yellow outfits recall the émigré Prince de Condé's livery, yet Louis shrugs off risk; he is recognized at Montmirail, Chaintrix and Châlons.
Dbvk5N9Pe84
At Sainte-Menehould postmaster Drouet recognizes the queen and the king from his face on paper money, and townsmen send him riding ahead to Varennes.
Dbvk5N9Pe84
Outside Varennes the promised fresh horses are missing; Drouet gallops past them, rouses the town, and grocer-magistrate Sauce and the militia halt the coaches.
